Creating Beautiful Violin Plots with ggplot2

R
ggplot2
Data Visualization
Tutorial
A step-by-step guide to evolving a basic violin plot into an advanced, publication-ready visualization
Author

Your Name

Published

October 14, 2025

Introduction

In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated violin plots using ggplot2. We’ll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.

Violin plots are excellent for visualizing distributions, combining the benefits of box plots and density plots to show the full shape of your data.

We’ll use the built-in diamonds dataset from ggplot2, which contains prices and attributes of nearly 54,000 diamonds.

Setup

First, let’s load the required packages and prepare our data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)  # Includes ggplot2, dplyr, and other essential packages
library(scales)     # For formatting axes and labels

# Prepare the data: filter for select diamond cuts
data_diamonds <- diamonds %>%
  filter(cut %in% c("Fair", "Good", "Very Good", "Premium", "Ideal")) %>%  # Use all cut levels
  mutate(cut = factor(cut, levels = c("Fair", "Good", "Very Good", 
                                      "Premium", "Ideal")))                 # Set factor order

# Preview the data
head(data_diamonds)
# A tibble: 6 × 10

Chart 1: Basic Violin Plot

Let’s start with a simple violin plot showing the distribution of diamond prices by cut quality.

ggplot(data_diamonds, aes(x = cut, y = price)) +  # Set up the plot with x and y variables
  geom_violin()                                    # Create violin plot

Code Explanation

Line 1: ggplot(data_diamonds, aes(x = cut, y = price)) - Initializes the plot with our diamond data, mapping cut quality to the x-axis and price to the y-axis

Line 2: geom_violin() - Adds violin shapes to the plot where the width represents the density of data points at each price level

What we have so far: A functional but basic violin plot. The distribution shapes are visible but the chart lacks context, color differentiation, and visual appeal.

Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement

Now we’ll improve the chart by adding color, internal box plots for reference points, and applying a clean theme with better labels.

What we’re adding in this evolution:

  • Color fill to distinguish each cut quality
  • Overlaid box plots showing median and quartiles
  • Improved axis labels and title for clarity
  • Clean theme to remove visual clutter
  • Transparency for better layering visibility
  • Professional color palette from ColorBrewer
ggplot(data_diamonds, aes(x = cut, y = price, fill = cut)) +      # Add fill aesthetic
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.7, trim = FALSE) +                         # Violin with transparency
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.1, fill = "white", 
               outlier.shape = NA) +                               # Narrow box plot overlay
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +                            # Apply color palette
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_dollar()) +                    # Format y-axis as currency
  labs(
    title = "Diamond Price Distribution by Cut Quality",           # Main title
    subtitle = "Violin plots showing full distribution with quartile overlay",  # Subtitle
    x = "Cut Quality",                                             # X-axis label
    y = "Price (USD)"                                              # Y-axis label
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +                                                # Clean, minimal theme
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),          # Bold title
    legend.position = "none"                                       # Remove redundant legend
  )

Code Explanation

Line 1: aes(x = cut, y = price, fill = cut) - Maps cut quality to both x-axis position and fill color for visual distinction

Line 2: geom_violin(alpha = 0.7, trim = FALSE) - Creates violin shapes with 70% opacity and extends tails to minimum/maximum values

Lines 3-4: geom_boxplot() - Adds narrow white box plots inside violins to show median, quartiles, and range, with outliers hidden since they’re already visible in the violin

Line 5: scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") - Applies a professional, colorblind-friendly palette from ColorBrewer

Line 6: scale_y_continuous(labels = label_dollar()) - Formats y-axis values as currency with dollar signs

Lines 7-12: labs() - Adds descriptive title, subtitle, and axis labels to provide context

Line 13: theme_minimal() - Applies a clean theme with minimal visual elements

Lines 14-17: theme() - Customizes title formatting and removes the legend since cut quality is already shown on x-axis

What we have now: A much more informative chart with color differentiation, clear reference points through box plots, and professional formatting. The currency formatting and clean theme make it presentation-ready.

Chart 3: Advanced Visualization

Let’s take it to the next level with jittered data points, sample size annotations, enhanced typography, and polished formatting suitable for publication.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

  • Individual data points (jittered and sampled for clarity)
  • Sample size annotations showing number of diamonds in each category
  • Custom color palette optimized for accessibility
  • Enhanced typography with refined spacing
  • Statistical reference line showing overall median
  • Data source caption for proper attribution
  • Refined spacing and margins for professional appearance
  • Better axis formatting with comma separators
# Calculate sample sizes and median for annotations
cut_summary <- data_diamonds %>%
  group_by(cut) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),                                       # Count per category
    median_price = median(price),                  # Median price
    .groups = 'drop'
  )

# Calculate overall median for reference line
overall_median <- median(data_diamonds$price)

# Sample data points for visualization (to avoid overplotting)
set.seed(123)
data_sample <- data_diamonds %>%
  group_by(cut) %>%
  slice_sample(prop = 0.05) %>%                    # Sample 5% of points per category
  ungroup()

# Define custom color palette (colorblind-friendly)
cut_colors <- c(
  "Fair" = "#E76F51",                              # Coral for lowest quality
  "Good" = "#F4A261",                              # Orange
  "Very Good" = "#E9C46A",                         # Yellow
  "Premium" = "#2A9D8F",                           # Teal
  "Ideal" = "#264653"                              # Dark blue for highest quality
)

ggplot(data_diamonds, aes(x = cut, y = price, fill = cut)) +
  # Add reference line for overall median
  geom_hline(yintercept = overall_median, 
             linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40", 
             linewidth = 0.6, alpha = 0.7) +
  # Violin plot layer
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.6, trim = FALSE, 
              color = "gray30", linewidth = 0.7) +
  # Box plot overlay
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, fill = "white", 
               outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.9,
               color = "gray30", linewidth = 0.5) +
  # Add jittered sample points
  geom_jitter(data = data_sample,
              width = 0.15, alpha = 0.2, size = 0.8,
              color = "gray20") +
  # Apply custom colors
  scale_fill_manual(values = cut_colors) +
  # Format y-axis with dollar signs and commas
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_dollar(scale = 1, prefix = "$"),
                     breaks = seq(0, 20000, by = 5000),
                     limits = c(0, 20000)) +
  # Add comprehensive labels
  labs(
    title = "Diamond Prices Vary Significantly Across Cut Quality Grades",
    subtitle = "Distribution analysis of 53,940 diamonds showing price ranges and density patterns",
    x = NULL,                                      # Remove x-axis label (obvious from plot)
    y = "Price (USD)",
    caption = "Data source: ggplot2 diamonds dataset | Dashed line indicates overall median price | Visualization: Your Name"
  ) +
  # Add sample size annotations
  geom_text(data = cut_summary,
            aes(x = cut, y = 19000, 
                label = paste0("n = ", format(n, big.mark = ","))),
            inherit.aes = FALSE,
            size = 3.2, fontface = "italic", 
            color = "gray30") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    # Title and text styling
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, 
                              margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "#5A6C7D", 
                                  margin = margin(b = 15)),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8.5, color = "#6C757D", 
                                hjust = 0, margin = margin(t = 15)),
    
    # Axis styling
    axis.title.y = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold", 
                                margin = margin(r = 10)),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10, color = "#2C3E50"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10.5),
    
    # Legend removal
    legend.position = "none",
    
    # Grid and panel styling
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),          # Remove vertical grid
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "#E9ECEF", linewidth = 0.5),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),            # Remove minor gridlines
    
    # Margins
    plot.margin = margin(15, 15, 15, 15)          # Add space around plot
  )
Warning: Removed 149 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_violin()`).

Code Explanation

Lines 2-9: Creates a summary dataframe with sample sizes and median prices for each cut category, used for annotations

Line 12: Calculates the overall median price across all diamonds to add as a reference line

Lines 15-19: Samples up to 200 diamonds per category to show individual data points without severe overplotting

Lines 22-28: Defines a custom color palette that progresses from warm (low quality) to cool (high quality) colors, optimized for colorblind accessibility

Line 30: ggplot() initializes the plot with cut mapped to both x-position and fill color

Lines 32-34: geom_hline() adds a dashed horizontal reference line at the overall median price for comparison

Lines 36-37: geom_violin() creates the violin shapes with transparency, custom border color, and full tail extension

Lines 39-41: geom_boxplot() overlays narrow white box plots showing quartiles and median with styled borders

Lines 43-45: geom_jitter() adds sampled individual data points with controlled horizontal spread and transparency

Line 47: scale_fill_manual() applies our custom color palette

Lines 49-51: scale_y_continuous() formats the y-axis with dollar signs, comma separators, and defined breaks

Lines 53-59: labs() adds comprehensive labels including an informative title that tells a story, descriptive subtitle with data context, and detailed caption with attribution and methodology notes

Lines 61-67: geom_text() adds sample size annotations at the top of each violin, formatted with comma separators for readability

Lines 68-93: Comprehensive theme customization including: - Enhanced typography with specific sizes, weights, and colors for hierarchy - Legend removal (since cut is mapped to x-axis) - Grid customization keeping only horizontal major gridlines - Proper margins for professional spacing

Final result: A publication-ready visualization that combines distribution density (violin), statistical summaries (box plot), individual observations (jittered points), and contextual information (sample sizes and reference line). The progressive color scheme and polished formatting make this suitable for academic papers, reports, or presentations.

Comparison: All Three Charts

Here’s a side-by-side view of our progression:

Context None Title & labels added Full context with subtitle, caption & sample sizes
Visual Appeal Plain gray violins Colored + professional theme Multi-layered + custom palette
Data Layers Violin only Violin + box plot Violin + box + points + reference line

Key Takeaways

Tip

Tips for Creating Better ggplot2 Violin Plots:

  1. Combine layers strategically - Violin + box plot is a powerful combination showing both distribution shape and statistical summaries

  2. Mind the sample size - For large datasets (>10,000 points), sample your data points when using geom_jitter() to avoid overplotting and file size issues

  3. Use trim = FALSE thoughtfully - This shows the full estimated distribution but can sometimes extend beyond your actual data range

  4. Add reference lines - Horizontal lines showing medians, means, or thresholds help viewers make comparisons

  5. Color with purpose - Use color gradients that match the ordering of your categories (e.g., cool to warm colors for low to high quality)

  6. Annotate sample sizes - Always show the number of observations per category so readers can assess reliability

  7. Consider log scales - For right-skewed data like prices, try scale_y_log10() to better show the full distribution

  8. Width matters - Adjust violin width with the scale parameter in geom_violin(): use "area" (default), "count", or "width"

  9. Box plot positioning - Keep box plots narrow (width = 0.1-0.15) so they don’t obscure the violin shape

  10. Export at high resolution - Use ggsave("plot.png", width = 10, height = 6, dpi = 300) for publication-quality images

Next Steps

Try applying these principles to other distribution visualizations:

  • Ridgeline plots for comparing many distributions
  • Beeswarm plots for smaller datasets where every point matters
  • Density plots for smoother distribution visualization
  • Grouped violin plots using facet_wrap() for additional categorical variables

Want to create grouped violin plots?

You can add a second grouping variable using position adjustments:

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = cut, y = price, fill = clarity)) +
  geom_violin(position = position_dodge(width = 0.9)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d() +
  theme_minimal()

This creates side-by-side violins for each combination of cut and clarity.

## Introduction

In this tutorial, we'll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated violin plots using `ggplot2`. We'll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.

Violin plots are excellent for visualizing distributions, combining the benefits of box plots and density plots to show the full shape of your data.

We'll use the built-in `diamonds` dataset from ggplot2, which contains prices and attributes of nearly 54,000 diamonds.

## Setup

First, let's load the required packages and prepare our data:

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)  # Includes ggplot2, dplyr, and other essential packages
library(scales)     # For formatting axes and labels

# Prepare the data: filter for select diamond cuts
data_diamonds <- diamonds %>%
  filter(cut %in% c("Fair", "Good", "Very Good", "Premium", "Ideal")) %>%  # Use all cut levels
```

## Chart 1: Basic Violin Plot

Let's start with a simple violin plot showing the distribution of diamond prices by cut quality.

```{r}
#| label: chart-basic
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5

ggplot(data_diamonds, aes(x = cut, y = price)) +  # Set up the plot with x and y variables
  geom_violin()                                    # Create violin plot
```

### Code Explanation

**Line 1:** `ggplot(data_diamonds, aes(x = cut, y = price))` - Initializes the plot with our diamond data, mapping cut quality to the x-axis and price to the y-axis

**Line 2:** `geom_violin()` - Adds violin shapes to the plot where the width represents the density of data points at each price level

::: {.highlight-box .info}
**What we have so far:**
A functional but basic violin plot. The distribution shapes are visible but the chart lacks context, color differentiation, and visual appeal.
:::

## Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement

Now we'll improve the chart by adding color, internal box plots for reference points, and applying a clean theme with better labels.

```{r}
#| label: chart-intermediate
```

```{r}
#| label: chart-advanced

# Define custom color palette (colorblind-friendly)
cut_colors <- c(
  "Fair" = "#E76F51",                              # Coral for lowest quality

  "Very Good" = "#E9C46A",                         # Yellow
  "Premium" = "#2A9D8F",                           # Teal

ggplot(data_diamonds, aes(x = cut, y = price, fill = cut)) +
  # Add reference line for overall median

  # Violin plot layer

  ) +
  # Add sample size annotations
  geom_text(data = cut_summary,
            aes(x = cut, y = 19000,
```

## Key Takeaways

::: {.callout-tip}
**Tips for Creating Better ggplot2 Violin Plots:**

1. **Combine layers strategically** - Violin + box plot is a powerful combination showing both distribution shape and statistical summaries

2. **Mind the sample size** - For large datasets (>10,000 points), sample your data points when using `geom_jitter()` to avoid overplotting and file size issues

3. **Use `trim = FALSE` thoughtfully** - This shows the full estimated distribution but can sometimes extend beyond your actual data range

4. **Add reference lines** - Horizontal lines showing medians, means, or thresholds help viewers make comparisons

5. **Color with purpose** - Use color gradients that match the ordering of your categories (e.g., cool to warm colors for low to high quality)

6. **Annotate sample sizes** - Always show the number of observations per category so readers can assess reliability

7. **Consider log scales** - For right-skewed data like prices, try `scale_y_log10()` to better show the full distribution

8. **Width matters** - Adjust violin width with the `scale` parameter in `geom_violin()`: use `"area"` (default), `"count"`, or `"width"`

9. **Box plot positioning** - Keep box plots narrow (width = 0.1-0.15) so they don't obscure the violin shape

10. **Export at high resolution** - Use `ggsave("plot.png", width = 10, height = 6, dpi = 300)` for publication-quality images

:::

---

## Next Steps

Try applying these principles to other distribution visualizations:

- **Ridgeline plots** for comparing many distributions
- **Beeswarm plots** for smaller datasets where every point matters
- **Density plots** for smoother distribution visualization
- **Grouped violin plots** using `facet_wrap()` for additional categorical variables

::: {.highlight-box .info}
**Want to create grouped violin plots?**

You can add a second grouping variable using position adjustments:

```r
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = cut, y = price, fill = clarity)) +
  geom_violin(position = position_dodge(width = 0.9)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d() +
  theme_minimal()
```

This creates side-by-side violins for each combination of cut and clarity.
:::
